status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.

summary: Your HbA1c of 6.5 falls in the diabetes range, and your BMI of 24.2 puts you in the overweight category, which together with your age of 55 are the main factors to focus on. These factors can affect how your body manages blood sugar over time. The most valuable next steps are getting your vitamin B12 levels and a cardiovascular risk assessment checked, since these were highlighted as priorities, along with staying consistent with regular physical activity and following a balanced eating pattern around your 1700 calorie target. Taking these steps now can help you build habits that support steady blood sugar levels going forward.

plan.portion_guidance: Fill half your bowl with non-starchy vegetables, one quarter with a plant protein like tofu or edamame, and one quarter with a whole grain such as brown rice, millet or soba noodles. Use a small handful for nuts and seeds, and a cup for soups or congee.
plan.hydration: Aim for about 8 glasses of water through the day. Unsweetened green tea is a good option between meals. Avoid sweetened plant milks and bottled tea drinks.

overweight BMI: moderate portions with vegetable-forward meals

exercise: Since you're already moderately active, aim to build toward at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity like brisk walking, cycling, or swimming, spread across most days.
Add muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days a week, such as bodyweight exercises, resistance bands, or light weights.
Increase intensity or duration gradually, listening to your body as you build endurance.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Start with 20-25 minutes of brisk walking 5 days a week, and build up to 30 minutes 5-6 days a week over the next month.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI falls in the overweight category, so gradually working toward a healthier weight range can help support better blood sugar management. Focus on balanced vegan meals with plenty of vegetables, whole grains, and plant-based proteins, alongside regular physical activity, rather than quick fixes.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep each night. Try to keep a consistent sleep and wake schedule, limit screens before bed, and create a cool, dark, quiet sleeping environment.
stress: Practice deep breathing exercises or guided meditation for 10 minutes a day to help calm your mind.
Consider regular mindfulness practices, like yoga or tai chi, which can also support physical activity goals.
Make time for enjoyable activities and social connections, which can help buffer daily stress.
behaviour_change: Keep a simple log of your meals, activity, and how you feel to help spot patterns and stay motivated.
Set small, achievable weekly goals rather than trying to change everything at once.
Since you don't smoke or drink, keep up these healthy habits as a strong foundation for your overall wellbeing.

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

preventive_actions: Schedule a vitamin B12 test and a cardiovascular risk assessment, since these were flagged as priorities for you
Aim for consistent moderate physical activity most days of the week to support healthy blood sugar levels
Work toward gradually reducing body weight toward a healthier range, which can ease pressure on blood sugar control
Keep meals balanced and mindful of portions to help stay near your 1700 calorie target
Track your HbA1c, fasting blood sugar, and post-meal blood sugar at the intervals your doctor recommends
Have your blood pressure and lipid profile checked regularly, since these interact closely with blood sugar management
